questions.stem: Where does Tara Westover grow up?
options: On Buck's Peak, a mountain in Idaho, where her father runs a scrapyard
On a cattle ranch in Montana, where her father works as a hired ranch hand
In a small town in Utah, where her father is a church bishop
On a commune in Oregon, where her family farms with other families
questions.explanation: Tara grows up on Buck's Peak in Idaho. Her father salvages scrap metal, and the children work in his junkyard from a young age.

questions.stem: What schooling does Tara have before university?
options: A few years at a public school, until her father takes her out of it
A full education at a church school in the nearest town to Buck's Peak
Lessons from a private tutor hired by her grandmother each summer
Almost none: she never attends school, and her home schooling fades away
questions.explanation: Tara's mother began home schooling, but it soon lapsed. The first classroom Tara ever sits in is at Brigham Young University.

questions.stem: Which best describes her father's beliefs?
options: He fears the government but wants his children to attend the public school
He follows mainstream church teaching and trusts the local authorities
He distrusts the government, doctors and schools, and prepares for the End of Days
He distrusts schools but takes the family to doctors whenever they fall ill
questions.explanation: Her father fears the government and the medical establishment. He stockpiles food, fuel and weapons for the collapse he expects.

questions.stem: Why does the story of the Weaver family at Ruby Ridge matter so much to her father?
options: It convinces him that the Weavers were reckless and brought it on themselves
It persuades him to give up his guns so that agents have no reason to come
It confirms his fear that federal agents will come for families like his
It convinces him to move his family closer to town for their own safety
questions.explanation: Ruby Ridge was a deadly 1992 siege by federal agents in Idaho. Tara's father tells it as proof the government attacks families, and as a child she imagines such an attack on her own family so vividly that it feels like a memory.

questions.stem: What happens when the year 2000 arrives?
options: Nothing: the world does not end as her father predicted, and he is crushed
The power fails across Idaho, and her father is proved right in public
Federal agents raid Buck's Peak, as her father always said they would
Her father sells off the family's stores, ashamed of having believed in Y2K
questions.explanation: Her father prepared for disaster at the millennium. When the new year arrives without incident, he sinks into a deep depression.

questions.stem: How are serious injuries in the family usually treated?
options: By a doctor from the church who visits Buck's Peak once each month
By driving to a specialist in Salt Lake City whenever needed
At home, with her mother's herbal remedies, instead of in hospital
At the hospital in town, where her mother works as a nurse
questions.explanation: Her mother is a herbalist and midwife. Burns, head injuries and wounds from car crashes and the junkyard are treated with tinctures and salves, often against all medical sense.

questions.stem: After her father is badly burned in an explosion, how is he treated?
options: He is flown to a burns unit, where doctors save his hands and face
He goes to hospital only after Tara calls an ambulance without asking
He is treated by Tyler, who has trained as a doctor at university
He refuses hospital, and the family nurse his burns at home for weeks
questions.explanation: Her father survives terrible burns treated only with home remedies. His recovery strengthens the family's faith in her mother's remedies.

questions.stem: Which brother first leaves for college and encourages Tara to do the same?
options: Tyler
Shawn
Luke
Tony
questions.explanation: Tyler goes to college against his father's wishes and urges Tara to study for the ACT, the test she needs to get into university.

questions.stem: Which best describes Shawn's treatment of Tara?
options: He teases her harshly but stops when their father steps in
He swings between protecting her and violently abusing her
He is violent towards Audrey but consistently protective of Tara
He bullies her as a child but changes once she leaves for BYU
questions.explanation: Shawn can be protective, but he is also violent and controlling towards her. This pattern, and the family's response to it, is at the centre of the memoir.

questions.stem: What happens when Tara asks about the Holocaust in a class at BYU?
options: She has studied it at home and gives a talk about it to the class
She has never heard of it, and the class reacts as if she is joking
She corrects her lecturer on a date, and the class is impressed
She refuses to discuss it because her father has forbidden it
questions.explanation: Tara asks what the word means because she has never learned about it. The moment shows how much her upbringing has kept from her.

questions.stem: Which professor at Cambridge praises Tara's work and urges her to believe in herself?
options: Professor Whitfield
Professor Ellison
Professor Steinberg
Professor Hargreaves
questions.explanation: On a study-abroad program at Cambridge, Professor Jonathan Steinberg praises her writing and encourages her ambitions. A BYU professor, Dr Kerry, had helped her join the program.

questions.stem: Which scholarship allows Tara to study at Cambridge after BYU?
options: The Marshall Scholarship
The Gates Scholarship
The Rhodes Scholarship
The Fulbright Scholarship
questions.explanation: Tara wins a Gates Scholarship to Cambridge. She later spends time at Harvard as a visiting fellow and completes her PhD in history at Cambridge.

questions.stem: Why do Tara's parents visit her at Harvard?
options: To bring her back to their beliefs and to Buck's Peak
To celebrate the completion of her doctorate in history
To ask her for money to save the family's struggling business
To tell her that Shawn has left the family for good
questions.explanation: Her parents come to reclaim her for their way of life. Tara refuses to accept their version of events.

questions.stem: Which event marks Tara's deepest break with her family?
options: Her father refuses to pay any of her fees at Cambridge or Harvard
Her father disowns her for accepting the Gates Scholarship to Cambridge
Her brother Tyler cuts her off after she publishes her first article
Her parents side with Shawn and deny her account of his violence
questions.explanation: When Tara speaks about Shawn's abuse, her parents and several siblings reject her account. Her mother, who once seemed to support her, sides with her father.

questions.stem: How does the memoir end?
options: Tara returns to Buck's Peak and wins back her place in the family
Tara and her father are fully reconciled at her graduation ceremony
Tara breaks with Tyler but makes her peace with both of her parents
Tara, now a historian, accepts that she must live apart from her parents
questions.explanation: Tara completes her PhD, keeps in touch with only some of her family and accepts that she cannot go back to the mountain as before. She remains estranged from her parents.

questions.stem: What does Tara come to suspect may explain some of her father's behaviour?
options: A brain injury
Severe deafness
Heart disease
Bipolar disorder
questions.explanation: Reading about bipolar disorder in a psychology class, Tara recognises her father in it. This changes how she understands his beliefs and moods.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures Tara's mother, Faye?
options: A trained nurse who quietly takes the children to doctors while her husband is away
A strict teacher who gives the children a thorough and structured home education
A loyal ally who leaves Buck's Peak with Tara once she learns about Shawn's violence
A skilled midwife and herbalist who at times supports Tara but sides with her father
questions.explanation: Faye is capable and at times loving, and she builds a successful herbal remedy business. But when the family divides, she takes her husband's side.

questions.stem: What does Tara's sister Audrey do after first standing up to Shawn with Tara?
options: She cuts Tara off, fearing she will lose the rest of the family
She stands by Tara for good and breaks with both of their parents
She reports Shawn to the police and gives evidence at his trial
She persuades their mother to leave their father and Buck's Peak
questions.explanation: Audrey and Tara confront their mother about Shawn together, but Audrey later withdraws and cuts Tara off. It shows the pressure on family members to choose a side.

questions.stem: What kind of text is Educated?
options: A history of Idaho, written as a series of essays
A memoir, a true account of the writer's own life
A novel loosely based on the writer's childhood
A biography of the writer, written by her brother
questions.explanation: Educated is a memoir, published in 2018. Westover tells her own story, and she acknowledges where others remember events differently.

questions.stem: Why are some family members in Educated given different names?
options: Westover uses pseudonyms to protect people's privacy
Westover changes names to signal that the people are fictional
The names are nicknames the siblings used for each other
Westover uses them to mark the events she has reimagined
questions.explanation: Several family members, including her parents and Shawn, appear under pseudonyms. It is common in memoirs about painful family events.

questions.stem: Brigham Young University, where Tara first studies, is run by which church?
options: The Roman Catholic Church
The Church of England
The Seventh-day Adventist Church
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
questions.explanation: BYU is a Latter-day Saint (Mormon) university in Utah. Tara's family are Mormon, but her father's version of the faith is far more extreme than most church members'.

questions.stem: How did Tara's parents respond to the memoir?
options: They praised the book but objected to the pseudonyms
Through a lawyer, they disputed much of her account
They accepted her account of Shawn in a public letter
They took legal action and stopped the book's sale
questions.explanation: Her parents' lawyer said they disputed her version of events, including her account of Shawn. The dispute is part of what readers weigh when thinking about memory and truth.

questions.stem: What does 'education' finally mean in the memoir?
options: Self-creation: gaining the power to think for herself and remake her life
Earning degrees that finally give her a respected place in the world
Learning to obey teachers, as she once obeyed her father on the mountain
Memorising facts, which she does to prove her family wrong about school
questions.explanation: Education is more than schooling for Westover. It is the process of forming her own mind and self, even when that changes her relationship with her family.

questions.stem: What does Educated suggest about memory and truth?
options: Memory is collective, so family members' accounts eventually agree
Memory is unreliable and personal, so different people's accounts can clash
Memory is reliable when it is written down soon after the events
Memory becomes trustworthy once a person has been formally educated
questions.explanation: Westover shows how her own memories shifted, and records where her siblings remember differently. The memoir is honest about the limits of what any one person can know.

questions.stem: What is the central conflict Tara faces as she becomes educated?
options: Her faith in God against the science she learns at university
Her ambition for a career against her family's need for money
Loyalty to her father against loyalty to her mother in their quarrels
Loyalty to her family against loyalty to her own understanding of the truth
questions.explanation: The more Tara learns, the more she sees her family differently. Staying loyal to them would mean denying what she knows, and the memoir explores the cost of choosing herself.

questions.stem: How does the memoir show the effect of a family's silence about abuse?
options: Silence protects the family and leads Shawn to change his behaviour
Speaking out leads her parents to confront Shawn about his violence
The abuse is kept secret from Tara, who learns of it only years later
Denial and silence let the violence continue and isolate those who speak
questions.explanation: When Tara and Audrey speak up, they are disbelieved or pressured to retract. The memoir shows how a family's denial protects the abuser rather than the victim.

questions.stem: What do Westover's footnotes do?
options: They give the scientific names of the herbs her mother used in remedies
They list the books Tara read at BYU to catch up on her education
They note where family members remember events differently from her
They translate the many Latin phrases used by her Cambridge professors
questions.explanation: Footnotes record other versions of events, such as how her siblings recall particular accidents. They show Westover being careful and honest about memory.

questions.stem: Westover kept journals, and she has said she once changed entries to match Shawn's version of events. What does this reveal?
options: That she planned the memoir from the very first journal entry
How pressure from her family led her to doubt her own memories
That her journals are the most reliable source in the memoir
That Shawn wrote parts of her journals while she was at BYU
questions.explanation: Rewriting her own record shows how deeply she had absorbed her family's version of reality. Learning to trust her own account is part of her education.

questions.stem: How is Educated structured?
options: In reverse order, beginning with her PhD and ending in her early childhood
In three parts, moving from the mountain to BYU to Cambridge and beyond
In two halves, one told by Tara and one told by her brother Tyler
In three parts, each named after a sibling who left the mountain
questions.explanation: Part One covers her childhood up to her acceptance at BYU, Part Two her years at BYU, and Part Three her life at Cambridge, Harvard and after.

questions.stem: Educated is told by the adult Westover looking back. What is the effect?
options: It means the reader sees events exactly as they seemed to the young Tara
It allows her siblings to correct her account within the main narrative
It hides the outcome, so the reader does not know she ever left Idaho
It lets her show what she understood as a child against what she knows now
questions.explanation: The retrospective narrator can show both the child's limited view and the adult's understanding. The gap between them is a measure of her education.

questions.stem: Professor Steinberg reminds Tara of the Pygmalion story. What does the allusion suggest?
options: It raises the idea of transformation, and who has the power to shape a person
It suggests Steinberg takes credit for creating the scholar she has become
It compares her father to a sculptor who loved his work too much to sell it
It suggests her education is only a change of surface manners and speech
questions.explanation: In the myth and in Shaw's play, a person is transformed by someone else. Tara's story asks whether she is being remade by others or is remaking herself.

questions.stem: The memoir's first chapter opens: 'My strongest memory is not a memory.' What does this signal?
options: That she will rely on family records rather than recollection
That memory is unreliable, a theme the whole memoir explores
That Tara's childhood memories are too painful for her to recall
That the memoir will be told from her mother's point of view
questions.explanation: Westover explains that this 'memory' is something she imagined from her father's story and came to remember as real. From the first line, she warns readers to think about how memory works.

questions.stem: The memoir ends with the words 'I call it an education.' What is 'it'?
options: The scholarship that paid for her studies in England
The change in herself that took her away from her family
The degree she received from Cambridge at her graduation
The home schooling her mother gave her on the mountain
questions.explanation: Westover lists words others might use for her change, such as betrayal, and chooses her own. The last line claims her transformation as an education in the fullest sense.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the prompt 'In Educated, learning comes at a terrible cost.' Discuss.
options: Westover shows that each step in her education pulls her further from the family she loves
Educated is a memoir by Tara Westover about growing up in Idaho and going to university
This essay will discuss the cost of learning in the memoir Educated by Tara Westover
Tara Westover went to BYU, then Cambridge and Harvard, and finally received a PhD
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence takes a position on the prompt and names what the paragraph will prove. The others retell, announce or state facts without making an argument.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Tara did not know what the Holocaust was.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: Add the name of the course and the year in which the class took place
List the other things Tara did not know when she arrived at BYU
Retell what the lecturer and the other students in the room said to her afterwards
Explain how the moment exposes how far her upbringing had kept the world from her
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what the evidence suggests. Linking the moment to the isolation of her childhood connects it to the memoir's ideas about education and control.
